The 1871 Portuguese legislative election takes place. The Historic Party wins a plurality of votes.
Fontes Pereira de Melo becomes prime-minister.
The 1874 Portuguese legislative election takes place. The Regenerator Party wins an absolute majority.
The Portuguese Republican Party is founded.
The Progressive Party is founded by merging the Historic and Reformist parties.
Marquis of Ávila becomes prime-minister for the 3rd time.
Fontes Pereira de Melo becomes prime-minister for the 2nd time.
Anselmo José Braamcamp becomes prime-minister.
The 1878 Portuguese legislative election takes place. The Regenerator Party keeps its absolute majority.
The 1879 Portuguese legislative election takes place. The Progressive Party wins an absolute majority.
António Rodrigues Sampaio becomes prime-minister.
The 1881 Portuguese legislative election takes place. The Regenerator Party wins an absolute majority.
Fontes Pereira de Melo becomes prime-minister for the 3rd time.
The 1884 Portuguese legislative election takes place. The Regenerator Party keeps its absolute majority.
Portugal takes part in the Berlin Conference.
The Pink Map is published, representing Portugal's claim of sovereignty over a land corridor connecting the Portuguese colonies of Angola and Mozambique during the Scramble for Africa.
José Luciano de Castro becomes prime-minister.
The 1887 Portuguese legislative election takes place. The Progressive Party wins an absolute majority.
Portugal and China sign the Sino-Portuguese Treaty of Peking, in the aftermath of the Second Opium War.
Luís I dies of neurosyphilis. Carlos I of Portugal, Luís' son, becomes king.
The 1889 Portuguese legislative election takes place. The Progressive Party keeps its absolute majority.
The British Government presents the Kingdom of Portugal with an Ultimatum.
António de Serpa Pimentel becomes prime-minister.
The 1890 Portuguese legislative election takes place. The Regenerator Party wins an absolute majority.
João Crisóstomo de Abreu e Sousa becomes prime-minister.

Republican insurrection in Porto. It is violently put down by the authorities, who afterwards institute a tight press censorship. Opponents of the government are accused of anarchism and exiled to the colonies.
Portugal signs the Anglo-Portuguese Treaty of 1891.
José Dias Ferreira becomes prime-minister.
The 1892 Portuguese legislative election takes place. The Regenerator Party keeps its absolute majority.
Ernesto Rodolfo Hintze Ribeiro becomes prime-minister.
The 1894 Portuguese legislative election takes place. The Regenerator Party again keeps its absolute majority.
The Battle of Coolela takes place. Portugal wins, defeating the Gaza Empire.
The 1895 Portuguese legislative election takes place. The Regenerator Party wins again, but the Progressive Party and the Portuguese Republican Party boycott the elections.
An arbitration by Italy finally establishes the international boundary between the British colony of Southern Rhodesia and Portugal's Mozambique colony.
José Luciano de Castro Pereira Corte-Real becomes prime-minister.
The 1897 Portuguese legislative election takes place. The Progressive Party wins a majority of votes.
Portugal signs the Treaty of Windsor with the United Kingdom, marking the restoration of Anglo-Portuguese relation.
The 1899 Portuguese legislative election takes place. The Progressive Party keeps its majority.
The Progressive Dissidence party is founded by Minister of Justice José Maria de Alpoim as a breakaway from the Progressive Party.
João Franco is appointed as Prime Minister of Portugal.
Big strike of the typographers.
Foundation of the Escola Superior Colonial (Superior Colonial School)
João Franco establishes a Dictatorship within the framework of the Monarchy.
Student's strike at the University of Coimbra.
The Portuguese Republican Party manages to elect all its candidates in the local elections of Lisbon.
Failed Republican revolutionary attempt. The conspirators are arrested.

Lisbon Regicide: King Carlos I of Portugal and his son and heir, prince Luis Filipe, Duke of Braganza, are killed in the Regicide of Lisbon by Alfredo Luís da Costa and Manuel Buíça, republicans of the Carbonária (the Portuguese section of the Carbonari).
Manuel II of Portugal, King Carlos's youngest son, becomes king.
King Manuel II of Portugal goes on a personal trip to Madrid, London and Paris.
The Portuguese Republican Party's Conference takes place in Setúbal, where the motion to accelerate the revolutionary movement to establish the Republic is approved.
In Lisbon a demonstration with more than 100,000 persons protests against the political and economical situation of the Monarchy.
Gafanha da Nazaré is founded by Prior Sardo and is bestowed to become a parish by the king Manuel II. Officially being the last town to receive such royal distinction by a Portuguese monarch.
Beginning of the Republican Revolution.
The Portuguese Republic is officially proclaimed in Lisbon. End of the Monarchy. Teófilo Braga is the president of the Provisional Government.
The last King of Portugal, Manuel II of Portugal, and the Portuguese Royal Family embark in Ericeira for exile in England.
Constituent National Assembly election, the Democratic Party wins a majority of 229 of the 234 seats.
Indirect presidential election. Manuel de Arriaga wins in the 1st round.
João Pinheiro Chagas is appointed prime-minister.
Augusto de Vasconcelos is appointed prime-minister.
East Timorese rebellion.
Duarte Leite is appointed prime-minister.
The royalist attack on Chaves, led by Henrique Mitchell de Paiva Cabral Couceiro, fails to reinstate the Monarchy.
Augusto de Vasconcelos becomes interim prime-minister.
Afonso Costa is appointed prime-minister.
Legislative election, the Democratic Party wins a plurality of 68 of the 153 seats in the Chamber of Deputies and 24 of the 71 seats in the Senate.
Bernardino Machado is appointed prime-minister.
Victor Hugo de Azevedo Coutinho is appointed prime-minister.
Pimenta de Castro is appointed prime-minister.
A revolt brings the end of Pimenta de Castro's government. A Constitutional Junta is formed.
João Pinheiro Chagas is appointed prime-minister for a second time, but he did not take office.
José de Castro is appointed prime-minister.
Indirect presidential election to select someone to complete Manuel de Arriaga's term. Teófilo Braga wins in the 1st round.
Indirect presidential election. Bernardino Machado wins in the 3rd round.
Legislative election, the Democratic Party wins a majority of 106 of the 163 seats in the Chamber of Deputies and 45 of the 69 seats in the Senate.
Afonso Costa is appointed prime-minister a second time.
António José de Almeida is appointed prime-minister.
The Portuguese Parliament accepts the participation of Portugal in the first world war, following the invitation of the British government to join the allied forces
The first members of the Portuguese Expeditionary Corps arrive in France.
Afonso Costa is appointed prime-minister a third time.
José Norton de Matos is appointed prime-minister.
Afonso Costa is appointed prime-minister a fourth time.
José Norton de Matos becomes interim prime-minister.
The December 1917 coup d'état marks the beginning of Sidónio Pais' rise to power. He leads the Military Junta.
Sidónio Pais (National Republican Party) wins the 1918 Portuguese general election. He ran unopposed.
The Armistice of 11 November 1918 marks the end of World War I.
Sidónio Pais is assassinated in the Rossio railway station. João do Canto e Castro succeeds Pais in leading the government.
Indirect presidential election. João do Canto e Castro wins in the 2nd round.
João Tamagnini Barbosa is appointed prime-minister.
The Monarchy of the North is proclaimed in Porto, and the restoration of the Portuguese monarchy lasts for about a month before being crushed by republican forces.
The Monarchy is proclaimed in Lisbon, in the Assault of Monsanto.
The Monarchic forces in Monsanto surrender, leading to the resignation of João Tamagnini two days later.
José Relvas is appointed prime-minister.
Domingos Leite Pereira is appointed prime-minister.
Legislative election, the Democratic Party wins a majority of 86 of the 163 seats in the Chamber of Deputies and 36 of the 71 seats in the Senate.
Alfredo de Sá Cardoso is appointed prime-minister.
Indirect presidential election. António José de Almeida wins in the 3rd round.in the 3rd round.
Francisco José Fernandes Costa is appointed prime minister. He did not take office and Alfredo de Sá Cardoso is re-appointed prime-minister.
Domingos Leite Pereira is appointed prime-minister a second time.
António Maria Baptista is appointed prime-minister.
José Ramos Preto is appointed prime-minister, after António Maria Baptista suddenly dies.
António Maria da Silva is appointed prime-minister.
António Granjo is appointed prime-minister.
Álvaro de Castro is appointed prime-minister.
Liberato Pinto is appointed prime-minister.
Bernardino Luís Machado Guimarães is appointed prime-minister a second time.
The Portuguese Communist Party was founded from the ranks of the Portuguese Maximalist Federation as the Portuguese Section of the Communist International.
Tomé de Barros Queirós is appointed prime-minister.
Legislative election, the Republican Liberal Party wins a plurality of 79 of the 163 seats in the Chamber of Deputies and 32 of the 71 seats in the Senate.
Indirect presidential election. Manuel Teixeira Gomes wins in the 3rd round.
António Granjo is appointed prime-minister a second time.
In the Bloody Night, then-head of Government António Granjo (Republican Liberal Party) is killed, along with other politician associates of his. Manuel Maria Coelho is appointed prime-minister.
Carlos Maia Pinto is appointed prime-minister.
Francisco Cunha Leal is appointed prime-minister.
Legislative election, the Democratic Party wins a plurality of 74 of the 163 seats in the Chamber of Deputies and 37 of the 70 seats in the Senate.
António Maria da Silva is appointed prime-minister a second time.
Portugal receives the Balfour Note, requiring that the loan Portugal had from the UK be paid back.
António Ginestal Machado is appointed prime-minister.
Álvaro de Castro is appointed prime-minister a second time.
Alfredo Rodrigues Gaspar is appointed prime-minister.
José Domingues dos Santos is appointed prime-minister.
Vitorino Guimarães is appointed prime-minister.
First failed coup attempt by Filomeno da Câmara.
Second failed coup attempt by Filomena da Câmara, now with the aid of Raul Esteves.
António Maria da Silva is appointed prime-minister a third time.
Failed coup attempt by Mendes Cabeçadas.
Domingos Leite Pereira is appointed prime-minister a third time.
Legislative election, the Democratic Party wins a majority of 83 of the 163 seats in the Chamber of Deputies and 39 of the 65 seats in the Senate.
Indirect presidential election. Bernardino Machado is elected President of the Republic for the 2nd time.
António Maria da Silva is appointed prime-minister a fourth time.
The General Manuel de Oliveira Gomes da Costa arrives at Braga with the purpose of initiating a Coup d'état.
The Republican Government and Prime Minister António Maria da Silva, knowing of the forthcoming coup, try to organise resistance believing the uprising can be defeated.
A Military coup d'état (henceforth known as the 28th May 1926 coup d'état) begins in Braga led by Gomes da Costa. Believing to have failed, Gomes da Costa announces his surrender.
The Portuguese Communist Party interrupts its 2nd Congress due to the political and military situation.
The Confederação Geral do Trabalho (national trade union centre) declares its neutrality in the military confrontations.

The Military Coup spreads to the rest of the country, by influence of Mendes Cabeçadas, Sinel de Cordes and Óscar Carmona, and establishes the Ditadura Nacional (National Dictatorship) against the democratic but unstable 1st Republic.
The Government of Prime Minister António Maria da Silva resigns.
The General Gomes da Costa is acclaimed in Porto.
The President of the Republic, Bernardino Machado, resigns.
José Mendes Cabeçadas Júnior becomes Prime Minister and President of the Republic.
António de Oliveira Salazar becomes Minister of Finance, he resigns 16 days after nomination.
The Congress of the Republic of Portugal (National Assembly) is dissolved by dictatorial decree.
All heads of Municipalities are substituted.
The Carbonária (the Portuguese section of the Carbonari) is banned.
All Political parties are banned.
General Gomes da Costa provokes a military coup.
General Gomes da Costa becomes Prime Minister.
Censorship is instituted.
General Gomes da Costa becomes President of the Republic.
General Gomes da Costa is obliged to step down and goes into exile.
General António Óscar de Fragoso Carmona, of the conservative military wing, becomes Prime Minister.
Failed military coup.
General António Óscar Carmona becomes President of the Republic.
The Police of Information of Lisbon, a Political Police, is created.
The Confederação Geral do Trabalho (national trade union centre) is dissolved.
Failed Republican coup attempt against the Ditadura Nacional in Porto (2 to 7) and Lisbon (7 to 9).
The Police of Information of Porto, a Political Police, is created.
Minimum School years are reduced from the 6th to the 4th grade; in all levels of non-university schooling students are divided by sex.
Failed right wing military coup.
Students demonstrate in Lisbon against the Ditadura Nacional.
General António Óscar de Fragoso Carmona remains President of the Republic.
Acordo Missionário (Missionary Agreement) between the Catholic Church and the Portuguese Republic, giving special status to the action of the Catholic Church in Portugal's colonies.
Failed Republican revolutionary attempt against the Ditadura Nacional.
The Portuguese Communist Party's Main Office is closed.
The Comissão de Propaganda da Ditadura (Commission for the Propaganda of the Dictatorship) is created.
The Police of Information of Porto and Lisbon are fused.
General José Vicente de Freitas becomes Prime Minister.
António de Oliveira Salazar becomes Minister of Finance for the 2nd time.
Failed Republican coup attempt against the Ditadura Nacional.
Catholic religious institutes are again permitted in Portugal.

The Portuguese Communist Party is reorganised under Bento Gonçalves. Adapting the Party to its new illegal status, the reorganisation creates a net of clandestine cells to avoid the wave of detentions.
Artur Ivens Ferraz becomes Prime Minister.

The Acto Colonial (Colonial Act) is published, defining the status of Portuguese colonies (Angola, Cabinda, Cape Verde, Portuguese Guinea, São Tomé and Príncipe, Mozambique, Portuguese India, Portuguese Timor and Macau).
The fundamental principles of the new regime are presented by António de Oliveira Salazar in the 4th anniversary of the 28 May Revolution.
Domingos da Costa e Oliveira becomes Prime Minister.
A Republican coup attempt against the Ditadura Nacional starts in Madeira. It would then expand to Azores and Portuguese Guinea, before dying out on 2 May 1931.
Failed Republican coup attempt against the Ditadura Nacional in Lisbon. There would be no remaining coup attempts during the Ditadura Nacional.
António de Oliveira Salazar becomes Prime Minister.
A new Constitution is approved in a false referendum, defining Portugal as a Corporative, Single Party and Multi-continental country (in Europe, Africa, Asia and Oceania).
A fascist-leaning right-wing Dictatorial regime entitled Estado Novo is installed.
The Single Party União Nacional (National Union) is created.
The Estatuto do Trabalho Nacional (Code of National Labour) is published, prohibiting all free trade unions.
A Political Police, the PVDE (Polícia de Vigilância e de Defesa do Estado; State Defence and Vigilance Police) is created.
Censorship, particularly of the Mass media, is systematic and generalised.
The Portuguese Communist Party's Secretary General Bento Gonçalves participates in the 7th Congress of the Comintern. Soon after returning to Portugal he is arrested by the Political Police PVDE.
The concentration camp for political prisoners of Tarrafal is created in the colony of Portuguese Cape Verde, under direct control of the political police PVDE.

The political police PVDE focuses its action against Communism and the underground Portuguese Communist Party. During this pre-World War II period, several Italian Fascist and German Nazi advisors came to Portugal, to help the PVDE adopt a model similar to the Gestapo.
Creation of the Mocidade Portuguesa (Portuguese Youth), a compulsory paramilitary youth organisation similar to the Hitler Youth.

Beginning of the Spanish Civil War; Portugal promptly supports Nationalist Spain under General Francisco Franco and sends military aid (the Battalion of the Viriatos) in their fight against the Spanish Republicans.
The female section of the Mocidade Portuguesa is created.
The Iberian Neutrality Pact is put forward by Salazar to Francisco Franco.
Salazar meets with Spanish dictator Francisco Franco.
Japanese forces invade Portuguese Timor in the Battle of Timor.
The Portuguese Communist Party's Secretary General Bento Gonçalves dies in the concentration camp of Tarrafal.

An international embargo on tungsten, which Portugal initially exported to both factions of World War II, and the longest drought on mainland Portugal lead to an economic recession that would last until 1945.
The Political Police PVDE is reorganised and renamed PIDE (Polícia Internacional e de Defesa do Estado; International Police for the Defence of the State).
The MUD (Movimento de Unidade Democrática – Movement of Democratic Unity) is created with official permission.
The MUD is banished.
The President António Óscar Carmona meets with Spanish dictator Francisco Franco.
Spanish dictator Francisco Franco receives a Doctorate honoris causa by the University of Coimbra.
In the (forged) Presidential elections, General Norton de Matos, backed by the oppositionist illegal organisation MUD tries and fail to win the Presidency of the Republic.
Portugal is a founding member of NATO.
For the first time, a Portuguese citizen is awarded with the Nobel Prize: Egas Moniz, with the Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine.
António de Oliveira Salazar becomes Provisional President of the Republic due to the death of President António Óscar de Fragoso Carmona.
Francisco Higino Craveiro Lopes becomes President of the Republic.
The Portuguese government overhauls the entire colonial system in an attempt to curb criticism on Portuguese Colonialism, all Portugal's colonies were renamed Portuguese Overseas Provinces.
Due to a bad harvest year and lower external demand for Portuguese goods, Portugal enters an economic recession that would last until 1953.
The Dadra and Nagar Haveli Portuguese enclave, dependent of Daman, is occupied by India.
Amílcar Cabral founds the PAIGC (Partido Africano da Independência da Guiné e Cabo Verde, African Party for the Independence of Guinea and Cape Verde).
The MPLA, Movimento Popular de Libertação de Angola (Popular Movement for the Liberation of Angola), is founded by Agostinho Neto.
Frente Nacional de Libertação de Angola (National Front for the Liberation of Angola), is founded as União das Populações do Norte de Angola (Union of the Populations of Northern Angola).
First live event of the Portuguese National Television and the beginning of the regular broadcasting. It was opened by the famous and former BBC war reporter, Fernando Pessa.
Américo Thomaz becomes President of the Republic.
Pijiguiti Massacre – Portuguese soldiers open fire on protesting dockworkers in Bissau (Portuguese Guinea), killing 50.
A group of ten Portuguese Communist Party members escaped from the high-security prison in Peniche. Among the escapees was Álvaro Cunhal.
Portugal is one of the founding member of the EFTA – European Free Trade Association.
The Prime Minister António de Oliveira Salazar takes on himself the office of Minister of National Defence and reorganises the Government to face the war in Africa.
The Portuguese Colonial War starts in Portuguese Angola with the attacks to the Prison, Police headquarters and Radio central in Luanda.
Attacks in northern Angola by the UPA (União do Povo Angolano; Union of the Angolan People), against Portuguese colonists and African populations, provoking hundreds of deaths.
Portugal joins the International Monetary fund.
The Indian army conquers Portuguese Goa.
The Indian army conquers Portuguese Daman and Diu.
The PAIGC Guerrilla warfare against the Portuguese begins with an abortive attack on Praia.
The Academic Crisis of '62 culminates in a huge student demonstration in Lisbon brutally repressed by the shock police, which caused hundreds of students to be seriously injured.
The FRELIMO – Frente de Libertação de Moçambique (Mozambican Liberation Front) is founded in Dar es Salaam (Tanzania).
The FLEC (Frente para a Libertação do Enclave de Cabinda; Front for the Liberation of the Enclave of Cabinda) is founded.
Amílcar Cabral and PAIGC declare full-scale war against the Portuguese in Portuguese Guinea.
The FRELIMO controls most of Northern Portuguese Mozambique.

The first Party Congress of the PAIGC takes place at liberated Cassaca, in which both the political and military arms of the PAIGC were assessed and reorganised, with a regular army (The People's Army) to supplement the guerrilla forces (The People's Guerillas).

6th Congress of the Portuguese Communist Party, one of the most important congresses in the Party's history, after Álvaro Cunhal released the report The Path to Victory – The tasks of the Party in the National and Democratic Revolution, which became an important document in the anti-dictatorship struggle.
The UNITA – União Nacional para a Independência Total de Angola (National Union for Total Independence of Angola) is founded by Jonas Savimbi.
The Salazar Bridge is inaugurated in Lisbon above the Tagus river. It is the longest suspension bridge in Europe and a replica (made by the same engineers) of the Golden Gate bridge in San Francisco.
By this time the PAIGC had carried out 147 attacks on Portuguese barracks and army encampments, and effectively controlled 2/3 of Portuguese Guinea.
Reorganisation of the Government.
Portugal begins a new campaign against the guerrillas in Portuguese Guinea with the arrival of the new governor of the colony, General António de Spínola.
António de Oliveira Salazar leaves the Government due to health problems.
Marcello das Neves Alves Caetano becomes Prime Minister.
The Single Party União Nacional is renamed Acção Nacional Popular (National Popular Action).
The Political Police PIDE is renamed DGS (Direcção Geral de Segurança, Directorate-General of Security).
Beginning of the Primavera Marcelista (Marcelist Springtime), a timid and failed opening of the regime.
Portugal invades Conakry, in the Republic of Guinea, 400 amphibious troops attacked the city and freed dozens of Portuguese Prisoners of war kept there by the PAIGC.
Death of António de Oliveira Salazar.
Amílcar Cabral, leader of the PAIGC, is assassinated in Conakry by a disgruntled former associate under influence of the Portuguese Political Police DGS.
Independence of Guinea-Bissau (Portuguese Guinea) is unilaterally declared.

A United Nations' General Assembly vote recognises the Independence of Guinea-Bissau, unprecedented as it denounced illegal Portuguese aggression and occupation and was prior to complete control and Portuguese recognition.
An economic recession starts, in the context of the international 1973–1975 recession.
The Carnation Revolution of 25 April puts an end to five decades of dictatorship.
The Carnation Revolution puts an end to the authoritarian regime of Estado Novo. Prime-minister Marcello Caetano exiled to Brazil
Independence is granted to all Portuguese colonies in Africa and independence is promised to Portuguese Timor.
A right-wing coup fails: A turn to the left in the revolution happens and major industries and big properties are nationalised by government

A meeting takes place in Haga (near Stockholm in Sweden) where the Committee for Friendship and Solidarity with Democracy and Socialism in Portugal is created. This Committee supported democratic trends in Portugal and opposed pro-soviet communist tendencies. In the meeting were present Olof Palme, Harold Wilson, Helmut Schmidt, Bruno Kreisky, Joop den Uyl, Trygve Bratteli, Anker Jørgensen, Yitzhak Rabin, Hans Janitschek, Willy Brandt, James Callaghan, François Mitterrand, Bettino Craxi and Mário Soares.
A coup removes far-left influence in politics.
East Timor (Portuguese Timor) is violently annexed by Indonesia.
A new Constitution is approved. The Constitutional Assembly disestablishes itself.
The Constitution of 1976 enters into force.
Jaime Ornelas Camacho becomes the first President of the Regional Government of Madeira.
Portugal requests International Monetary Fund aid for the first time since joining in 1961, in consequence of the 1973–1975 recession.
Prime minister Francisco Sá Carneiro and the Minister of Defence Amaro da Costa died in the 1980 Camarate plane crash, in strange circumstances.
An economic recession starts in Portugal, within the context of the early 1980s recession. It would last until around 1984.
Carlos Lopes wins the first Olympic gold medal for Portugal in the Los Angeles '84 marathon.
Portugal becomes a member of the European Economic Community, today's European Union'.
Portugal and China sign the Sino-Portuguese Joint Declaration establishing the process and conditions of the transfer of Macau from Portuguese rule to the People's Republic of China.
An economic recession starts in Portugal, within the context of the early 1990s recession, which affected most of the Western world. It would last until 1993.

The 1995 Portuguese legislative election would bring an end to 10 years of Social Democratic Party (PSD) rule by Aníbal Cavaco Silva. After the only two elections in which a party or pre-electoral coalition ever received more than 50% of votes since the Estado Novo, PSD lost with 34.1% of votes to PS' 43.8%.
Lisbon organises the World's Fair Expo '98.

In the first Portuguese abortion referendum, the proposal to allow the abortion until 10 weeks of pregnancy is rejected by 50.91% of the voters. This is the first referendum in the History of the Portuguese democracy.
For the very first time, a Portuguese Language author is awarded with the Nobel Prize of Literature: José Saramago.

in the regionalisation referendum, a proposal to establish, in mainland Portugal, 8 administrative regions and to disestablish the 18 districts, is rejected in the polls: in the first question, the simple institution of the administrative regions is rejected by 60.67% of the voters; in the second question, the proposal to create 8 regions is rejected by 60.62% of the voters. This is the first referendum in the History of Portugal to have more than 1 question.
Macau, the last overseas Portuguese colony, is returned to China
Hintze Ribeiro Bridge disaster: 59 people die in the collapse of an old bridge on the Douro river. Hours after the accident, Jorge Coelho, Minister of Transportation, resigns.
Portugal adopts the euro as currency.
2004 European Football Championship is held in Portugal.
The 2006 Dakar Rally, the longest and, arguably, the hardest off-road rally in the world starts in Lisbon.

In the second Portuguese abortion referendum, almost 9 years after the first, the proposal to allow the abortion until 10 weeks of pregnancy is now approved by 59.25% of the voters. The law is published in April.
The law that allows the same-sex marriage is approved by the Portuguese President of the Republic, Aníbal Cavaco Silva.

In 2010, the official infant mortality rate was 2.53 per mil, the lowest ever recorded in Portugal (1.6‰ below the UE-27, 2010 average), placing the country among the top-5 in the European Union in this particular value of Human Development.
Portugal national football team wins the 2016 UEFA European Football Championship, in Stade de France in Paris, France.
Salvador Sobral wins the 62nd edition of the Eurovision Song Contest, with the song Amar pelos dois, composed by Luísa Sobral, in Kyiv, Ukraine.
Lisbon hosts the 63rd edition of the Eurovision Song Contest, after Portugal's win in the previous year.
The arrival date of COVID-19 in Portugal.
Roman General Julius Caesar invades and conquers the lands of the Belgae: Battle of the Sabis; Siege of the Atuatuci
Julius Caesar campaigns unsuccessfully against the coastal tribes of the Morini and Menapii.
Julius Caesar subdues the Morini.
Ambiorix's revolt under Ambiorix and Cativolcus.
Punitive campaigns subdue Nervii and Treveri; exterminate Eburoni.
Julius Caesar completes writing Commentarii de Bello Gallico, his account of his campaigns in Gaul.
Marcus Nonius Gallus suppresses revolt among Treveri.
Augustus creates the province Gallia Belgica.
Probable origins of the city of Tongeren.
Augusta Treverorum becomes a city.
Nero Claudius Drusus, commander in chief of Roman forces in Gallia Belgica, has a series of canals dug in the Rhine–Meuse–Scheldt delta.
Probable origins of the city of Aarlen.
Nero Claudius Drusus dies after falling from his horse. Command of Rome's northern armies passes to Tiberius.
Monument honouring Tiberius erected in Bagacum.
Germanicus becomes commander of the Roman army of the Rhine.
Roman invasion of Germany under command of Germanicus launched from Fectio in Gallia Belgica.
Death of Germanicus.
Treveri revolt at high taxes.
Galba becomes commander of the armies in Lower Germany.
Gnaeus Domitius Corbulo becomes commander of the armies in Lower Germany. Orders canals dug in the Rhine–Meuse–Scheldt delta.
Roman law replaces customary law in Gallia Belgica; druids outlawed; Gaulish aristocracy given senatorial rank.
Armies of the Rhine proclaim Aulus Vitellius as emperor.
Treveri, Menapii, Nervii and Tungrii come out in support of the Batavian Revolt, some under compulsion.
Pliny the Elder starts writing his Historia Naturalis, book 4 of which contains a description of Gallia Belgica.
Northern border fortified with series of castra.
Domitian restructures provinces of the Roman Empire: Gallia Belgica divided into the provinces of Belgica Prima, Belgica Secunda, Germania Superior and Germania Inferior.
Chauci launch maritime raids on the coasts of Gallia Belgica.
Carausius, a Menapian general in the Roman army, declares himself emperor of Britain and Gaul.
Death of Carausius, brings the end of the Carausian revolt 3 years later.
Servatius, bishop of Tongeren, attends the Council of Serdica.
Land south of the Rhine delta ceded to Frankish foederati
Servatius, bishop of Tongeren, attends the Council of Ariminum.
Salian Franks take possession of Tournai.
Childeric I buried in Tournai.
Sigebert I inherits the Frankish kingdom of Austrasia.
Death of Gertrude of Nivelles
Death of Amandus.
Murder of Dagobert II in the Ardennes Forest.
Pepin of Herstal and his wife Plectrude found what will become the Abbey of Saint-Hubert.
Death of Begga.
Death of Lambert of Maastricht: murdered at a site that would become Liège.
See of Maastricht moved to the location of Lambert of Maastricht's murder, now Liège.
Death of Hubertus, Bishop of Liège.
Birth of Charlemagne, first Holy Roman Emperor.
Louis the Pious confirms the liberties granted to St Bavo's Abbey by Charlemagne (oldest extant original charter in a Belgian archive).
First recorded Viking raid on the Flemish coast.
The remains of St Hubert (died 727) installed in the monastery that would become the Abbey of Saint-Hubert.

Treaty of Verdun divides the Carolingian Empire between the three sons of Louis the Pious: Lothair I, Louis the German and Charles the Bald, creating the kingdom of Middle Francia (including most of the Low Countries) for Lothair and assigning Flanders to Charles the Bald.
Norsemen raid Flanders.
Treaty of Prüm divides Middle Francia into the Kingdom of Lotharingia (including most of the Low Countries), the Kingdom of Provence and the Kingdom of Italy.
Treaty of Meerssen partitions Lotharingia (including most of the Low Countries) between East Francia (Germany) and West Francia (France).
Norsemen raid Taxandria.
Norsemen raid Tournaisis.
Norsemen plunder Cambrai and encamp near Maastricht, extorting tribute from Maastricht, Tongeren, Liège, Sint-Truiden, Malmedy, Stavelot, and Prüm.
Norse invaders defeated in Battle on the Dijle.
Holy Roman Emperor Arnulf of Carinthia appoints his illegitimate son Zwentibold as king of Lotharingia.
Zwentibold slain by Count Reginar I of Hainault; Lotharingia reincorporated into East Francia.
Bishop of Liège granted right to levy a toll in Maastricht.
Count Reginar I of Hainault appointed margrave of Lotharingia; historically regarded as the first Duke of Lorraine.
Death of Reginar, Duke of Lorraine, at his palace in Meerssen; succeeded by his son Giselbert.
Death of Baldwin II, Margrave of Flanders at Blandijnberg; succeeded by his son Arnulf.
Henry the Fowler invades Lotharingia and receives oaths of loyalty from the local aristocracy.
Gilbert, Duke of Lorraine, attends the coronation of Otto I in Aachen.
Battle of Andernach: death of Gilbert, Duke of Lorraine; end of independence of Lotharingia (referred to as "Belgica" in the 10th-century histories of Richer of Rheims).
Saint-Ghislain Abbey reformed by Gérard of Brogne
Death of Isaac, Count of Cambrai; powers of count transferred to Fulbert, Bishop of Cambrai.
Bruno the Great, Archbishop of Cologne, appointed Duke of Lotharingia.
Hungarian attackers raid Lower Lotharingia, besiege Cambrai.
Bruno the Great divides Lotharingia into Upper Lotharingia (the later Duchy of Lorraine) and Lower Lotharingia (the later Duchy of Lothier).
Death of Gérard of Brogne.
Godfrey I, Duke of Lower Lorraine, dies in Italy; no immediate successor.
Death of Arnulf I, Count of Flanders; succession of Arnulf II, Count of Flanders
Otto I, Holy Roman Emperor, confirms Godfrey of Lower Lotharingia's gift to Saint-Ghislain Abbey of 18 mansi of land in Villers-Saint-Ghislain.
Death of Bruno the Great, Duke of Lotharingia.
Lothar, King of the Franks, confirms the possessions of St. Peter's Abbey, Ghent, including those bequeathed by Arnulf I, Count of Flanders, and contested by his heirs.
Richar, Count of Mons, appointed Duke of Lower Lotharingia.
Richar, Duke of Lower Lotharingia, dies; no immediate successor.
Otto II, Holy Roman Emperor, appoints Charles, brother of Lothair of France, as Duke of Lower Lotharingia.

Otto II, Holy Roman Emperor, confirms all previous endowments to Notker, Bishop of Liège, and issues a general immunity for the bishopric's lands: beginning of the establishment of the Prince-Bishopric of Liège.
Otto III, King of Germany, endows Notker, Bishop of Liège, with the County of Huy: full establishment of the Prince-Bishopric of Liège.
Death of Arnulf II, Count of Flanders; succession of Baldwin IV, Count of Flanders.
Death of Hildegard of Flanders, daughter of Arnulf II, Count of Flanders, and wife of Dirk II, Count of Holland.
Baldrick II succeeds Notger as prince-bishop of Liège

Battle of Vlaardingen: imperial forces commanded by Godfrey II, Duke of Lower Lorraine, and Baldrick II, bishop of Liège, defeated by the army of Dirk III, Count of Holland. Baldrick died after a sudden illness on the journey; Godfrey was captured in the battle.
Wolbodo consecrated bishop of Liège.
Durandus succeeds Wolbodo as prince-bishop of Liège
Reginard succeeds Durandus as prince-bishop of Liège
Death of Baldwin IV, Count of Flanders; succession of Baldwin V, Count of Flanders
Nithard succeeds Reginard as prince-bishop of Liège
Wazo succeeds Nithard as prince-bishop of Liège
Baldwin V, Count of Flanders, seizes control of the imperial castle at Ename
Theodwin succeeds Wazo as prince-bishop of Liège
Forces of Theodwin of Liège defeat forces of Dirk IV, Count of Holland, killing Dirk and restoring imperial authority in the Rhine delta.
Baldwin V, Count of Flanders, becomes regent of France
Ename Abbey founded
Theodwin of Liège grants city rights to Huy, the oldest such charter to survive from what is now Belgium.
Death of Baldwin V, Count of Flanders; succession of Baldwin VI, Count of Flanders
Genealogia comitum Flandrensium compiled.
Death of Baldwin VI, Count of Flanders; succession of Arnulf III, Count of Flanders
Battle of Cassel between Robert the Frisian and his nephew, Arnulf III, Count of Flanders. Arnulf was killed in the battle and Robert succeeded him as count.
Pope Gregory VII issues bull of protection for the Abbey of Saint-Hubert.
Pope Gregory VII writes to Theodwin, bishop of Liège, urging him to leave the abbot of Saint-Hubert unmolested.
Death of Theodwin of Liège.
Pope Gregory VII issues bull of protection for Watten Abbey.
Adela of Flanders marries Canute IV of Denmark
Traditional date of the first apparition of Our Lady of Tongre.
Adela of Flanders, queen consort of Denmark, returns to the Low Countries after her husband's murder
Godfrey of Bouillon becomes Duke of Lower Lorraine
Death of Robert I, Count of Flanders; succession of Robert II, Count of Flanders
Godfrey of Bouillon, Duke of Lower Lorraine, sets off as one of the leaders of the First Crusade.
Death of Godfrey of Bouillon
Baldric of Noyon, Bishop of Tournai, awards the right of presentment for Tielt to the chapter of St Salvator in Harelbeke.
St Michael's church, Hekelgem becomes a dependency of Affligem Abbey.
Godfrey I, Count of Louvain, invested as Duke of Lower Lotharingia in Worms Cathedral.
The hermit Ligerius founds a community that would become Ten Duinen Abbey (the Abbey of Dunes).
Death of Robert II, Count of Flanders; succession of Baldwin VII, Count of Flanders
Death of Baldwin VII, Count of Flanders; succession of Charles I, Count of Flanders (Charles the Good)
Godfrey I, Count of Louvain confirms the agreement of Ava of Waver and her sons with the priory of Forest, transferring ownership of an allod in Woluwe.
Murder of Charles the Good, Count of Flanders
Albero I of Louvain, prince-bishop of Liège, dies; succeeded by Alexander of Jülich
Foundation of Park Abbey.
Godfrey I, Count of Louvain, dies; succeeded by Godfrey II
Siege of Bouillon Castle by Albero, prince-bishop of Liège.
Godfrey II, Count of Louvain dies; succeeded by Godfrey III
Pope Eugene III confirms Wibald, Abbot of Stavelot and Malmedy, in possession of the goods of the abbey.
Henry II of Leez, Bishop of Liège, confirms Affligem Abbey in possession of its property in the diocese of Liège.
Godfrey III, Count of Louvain, takes Grimbergen

Henry the Blind, Count of Namur and of Luxembourg, being childless, names his sister Alice of Namur with her husband Baldwin IV, Count of Hainaut, and their son Baldwin, as heirs of all his allodial possessions, "with sod and twig", retaining usufruct during his own lifetime.
Henry II of Leez, prince-bishop of Liège, dies
Rudolf of Zähringen becomes prince-bishop of Liège
Death of Thierry, Count of Flanders; succession of Philip of Alsace as count of Flanders
Baldwin IV, Count of Hainaut, dies; succeeded by Baldwin V
Gislebert of Mons becomes chancellor to Baldwin V, Count of Hainaut.
Godfrey III, Count of Louvain, departs for Jerusalem

Henry the Blind, Count of Namur and of Luxembourg, being childless, names his nephew, Baldwin V, Count of Hainaut, already heir to all his allodial possessions, as heir equally to all his feudal possessions, "with sod and twig", retaining usufruct during his own lifetime.
Saint Lambert's Cathedral, Liège, destroyed by fire.
birth of Ermesinde, later countess of Luxembourg, only child of Henry the Blind. As a female heir she would inherit his allodial possessions, but not his feudal possessions.
Godfrey III, Count of Louvain dies; succeeded by Henry I, Duke of Brabant
Death of Philip of Alsace, Count of Flanders; succession of his daughter Margaret I, Countess of Flanders, and her husband and co-ruler Baldwin V, Count of Hainaut
Murder of Albert of Louvain, prince-bishop of Liège, by supporters of Emperor Henry VI
Relics of Saint Alena enshrined in Forest Priory.
Peace treaty between Henry I, Duke of Brabant and Baldwin V, Count of Hainaut, ending twelve years of conflict between the Duchy of Brabant and the County of Hainaut.
Death of Baldwin V, Count of Hainaut; succession of his son Baldwin VI as count of Flanders and Hainaut
Henry I, Duke of Brabant, departs for Jerusalem.
Baldwin VI, Count of Hainaut, donates all his possessions in the village of Horrues to the collegiate church of Soignies to endow a Lady chapel and a chantry.
Battle of Adrianople: Baldwin I of Constantinople, count of Flanders and Hainaut, captured by the Bulgarians
Henry I, Duke of Brabant, marries Marie of France in Soissons.
Battle of Bouvines: decisive French victory against the forces of Ferdinand, Count of Flanders, Henry I, Duke of Brabant, and Otto IV, Holy Roman Emperor. Count of Flanders carried captive to Paris.

Guy of Saint-Pol and his brother, Hugo of Saint-Pol, stand surety for a loan of 3693 pounds borrowed from citizens of Arras by Daniel, Lord of Béthune: an early example of the use of French rather than Latin in legal documents.
Henry I, Duke of Brabant, issues charter of city rights for Brussels.
Ferdinand, Count of Flanders and Joan, Countess of Flanders release inhabitants of the Brugse Vrije from the feudal relief of "best beast".
Henry I, Duke of Brabant, died; succeeded by Henry II
Statutes of the Ghent Leper Hospital translated from Latin: the earliest known example of a legal document entirely in Dutch.
Charters of the city of Ghent translated into Dutch.
Benedictine priory at Vorst, a dependency of Affligem Abbey, becomes the independent Forest Abbey.
Pope Innocent IV authorizes the canons regular of St Augustine to establish a grammar school in Leuven.
Henry II, Duke of Brabant, died; succeeded by Henry III
Gothic choir of Tournai Cathedral completed
Henry III, Duke of Brabant, dies; succeeded by Henry IV

Margaret of Constantinople, Countess of Flanders, impounds wares of English merchants in Flanders in retaliation for their king's non-payment of a money fief, sparking a trade war between Flanders and England.
Henry IV, Duke of Brabant, died; succeeded by John I
Treaty of Montreuil-sur-Mer between Edward I of England and Guy, Count of Flanders, ending four years of economic warfare and providing for free movement of merchants between their territories.
Future John II, Duke of Brabant, born.

Guy de Thourout does homage to Guy, Count of Flanders for lands in Wervik, Reninge and Rollegem. He also held land in Menen and Rekkem, a manor in Varsenare, and owned a number of houses within the city of Ypres.
Battle of Worringen
Aldermen of Nieuwpoort accept the mediation of Guy, Count of Flanders in their dispute with the abbeys of Duinen and Bourbourg concerning a dyke built near the town.
John I, Duke of Brabant, died; succeeded by John II
John II, Duke of Brabant, recognises that Affligem Abbey by immemorial custom has the right to appoint a panel of seven aldermen for the village of Hekelgem.
Edward I of England grants Flemish merchants the right to buy wool for export anywhere in the British Isles, rather than being limited to the wool staple.
Treaties of alliance between Philip IV of France and John of Avesnes, Count of Hainaut, culminate in a trade treaty allowing merchants from Hainaut to trade freely in the kingdom of France.
Battle of the Golden Spurs: Flemish forces defeat knights of Philip IV of France near Kortrijk
Aldermen of the city of Namur authorize formation of a butchers' guild with militia obligations, requiring members to arm themselves, follow their own banner, and bury their own dead.

The Charter of Kortenberg finalised at Kortenberg Abbey, establishing fundamental rights for the inhabitants of the Duchy of Brabant such as no punishment without due process. Council of four knights and ten representatives of the boroughs established (beginnings of representative institutions in the duchy).
Henry of Luxembourg died in Buonconvento while besieging Siena, reputedly of poison put in the chalice during mass.
Works begins on a new cloth hall in Leuven, which is now University Hall.
Joanna of Brabant born.
Rebellion of the commoners in maritime Flanders, sparked by Louis I, Count of Flanders, ceding Sluis to John I, Marquis of Namur.
Pope John XXII provides a dispensation for the marriage of Philippa of Hainault and Edward III of England. The marriage itself took place by proxy in Valenciennes in October.
Marriage of Philippa of Hainault and Edward III of England celebrated in York Minster.
Battle of Cassel: Philip VI of France defeats Flemish rebels led by Nicolaas Zannekin.

Treaty of mutual support between John III, Duke of Brabant and Louis I, Count of Flanders, and the cities subject to them, providing for offensive and defensive alliance and free trade between their territories.
Battle of Sluys
Jacob van Artevelde killed in Ghent.

The boroughs of the Duchy of Brabant and the Duchy of Limburg undertake to remain united under a single prince after the death of John III, Duke of Brabant, not allowing the territory to be divided among his heirs.
Joyous Entry of 1356: Joanna, Duchess of Brabant and her husband Wenceslaus I of Luxembourg sign the great charter of liberties of the Duchy of Brabant.
Extirpation of small Jewish population of Brabant after accusations of profaning eucharistic hosts.
Ghent Revolt led by Philip van Artevelde begins
Battle of Beverhoutsveld – men of Ghent take Bruges and gain control over most of the county of Flanders
Battle of Dunkirk

Louis II, Count of Flanders, last count of the House of Dampierre, dies; succeeded by his daughter Margaret III, Countess of Flanders, whose husband Philip the Bold ruled on her behalf: beginning of period of Burgundian rule in the Low Countries
Peace of Tournai ends the Ghent Revolt
Philip the Bold founds the Lille Chamber of Accounts to audit the accounts of his functionaries in the county of Flanders.
Oldest record of the incorporation of the Brussels guild of painters, goldbeaters and glassmakers.
John of Bavaria elected Prince-Bishop of Liège (resigned 1418).
Joanna, Duchess of Brabant secretly relinquishes possession of the Duchy of Brabant to her niece, Margaret of Male, and offspring thereof.
John of Bavaria, bishop-elect of Liège, writes to Philip the Bold to intercede for merchants from Liège arrested by the officers of Rethel.
John the Fearless takes fiscal measures to pay Alexander Stewart, Earl of Mar's archers joining him on the Liège campaign. (Letter bearing only known surviving signature of John the Fearless).
Suppression of the Homines Intelligentiae in Brussels.
Philip the Good transfers usufruct of the County of Namur to John of Flanders, Lord of Béthune, for the duration of his life.
Pope Martin V issues papal bull founding University of Leuven.
Tapestry weavers of Oudenaarde form the Guild of St Barbara.
Tournament held on the main square in Leuven in the presence of Philip the Good, Duke of Burgundy and Brabant.
Guilds of Ghent take up arms against the Count of Flanders, Philip the Good.
Philip the Good declares war on the city of Ghent.
Battle of Gavere: forces of Philip the Good defeat rebels of Ghent, ending their rebellion.
The Feast of the Pheasant, a banquet given by Philip the Good, Duke of Burgundy, held in Lille.
Tower of St. Peter's Church, Leuven, catches fire.
